title: Potential of Legumes in Mitigating Environmental Emissions of Milk Production
content: Dairy cattle is a central part of Finnish agriculture, but the environmental emissions of animal production, such as nitrogen emissions increasing eutrophication and methane emissions contributing toward the climate change, are an important issue. One way to diversify farming and decrease the environmental impact of feed production is to utilise biological nitrogen binding by using more legumes in dairy cow diets. The objective of this thesis was to investigate how legumes, specifically faba bean and red clover, affect nitrogen use efficiency in milk production and ruminal methane emissions.

title: DOPAGuard won the HealthBIO 2026 Pitching Competition! 🎉
content:
The Pitching Competition brought together eight teams with very different approaches to solving important healthcare challenges. The event showcased a wide range of strong science, ambitious ideas, and innovative technologies aimed at improving health and healthcare. 

The competition was part of HealthBIO 2026 in Turku, which celebrated its 20th edition and brought together experts, companies, investors, and other key actors from Finland and internationally.

For DOPAGuard, this recognition means a lot. We are working to build the next generation of levodopa protection for Parkinson’s disease, and moments like this help us bring that story to a wider life science and investment community. The pitch takes five minutes. The science behind it has taken years. It feels particularly good to see that work, and the idea behind DOPAGuard, resonate outside our own team.

title: Mitä ruis ja tattari kertovat keskiajan ihmisten elämästä? Tutkimukselle ERC-rahoitus
content:
The PlantStories project investigates the significance of rye and buckwheat to people in Northern Europe in the Middle Ages, from 1100 to 1600. The project investigates why these crops specifically became staples and how their cultivation and use were influenced not only by the environment, but also by cultural choices, traditions and societal change.

The project helps to understand how humans have adapted to societal and environmental changes over the centuries, adapting their food production and plant use accordingly. 

The history of plants cultivated in the past also provides a long-term perspective on the current discussion on the sustainability of food systems and diversified agriculture, as well as why some plants remain important across generations. 

“Food production cannot be explained solely by climate and growth conditions. In addition, culture, traditions and human choices have played a key role in the cultivation and consumption of plants,” says Lempiäinen-Avci.

title: Climate change won’t simply shrink marine life
content:
Research led by scientists at the University of Louisiana at Lafayette challenges a long-held assumption about the effects of climate change on marine life: warmer oceans won’t simply make animals smaller.

The study was led by , who conducted the research as a postdoctoral researcher in the UL Lafayette laboratory of senior author Dr. Craig McClain. Trindade-Santos is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki.

Researchers analyzed more than 23,000 species of marine mollusks — the group that includes clams, oysters, snails, squid, octopuses and chitons — and found that body size is projected to decline in most ocean regions by 2100. But those changes are far from uniform. Some groups could shrink dramatically, while others are projected to grow larger.

The peer-reviewed study, “,” was published Aug. 31 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, one of the world’s most-cited multidisciplinary scientific journals.

title: What Did it Mean to Be A Man in Ancient Western Asia?
content:
This question was at the heart of a workshop on 27th-28th August, titled . The hybrid workshop included 20 papers, including a keynote from Professor Martti Nissinen (University of Helsinki). All questioned what it meant to be a man in Mesopotamian, Egyptian, and biblical sources.

The topics were diverse and included discussions on how inheritance practices determined survival in sieges (Uroš Matic); how hospitality practices were gendered (Anne Katrine de Hemmer Gudme); and how institutions could manipulate masculinities to ensure the king lived in moments of crisis (Kelsie Ehalt). 

One theme permeated throughout the workshop: there was (and is) no single way to be a man. Different cultures had different ideas of what being a man meant. We even saw how the boundaries between modern ideas of a gender binary were blurred in ancient cultures. For example, Individuals could be depicted in images as women, but have male names in Achaemenid Egypt (Matheus Treuk). Masculinities were malleable, and changed depending on context, culture, and other aspects of identity.

title: “Ilman pölyttäjiä maailma olisi ankea ja väritön” – Uusi näyttely avaa oven pölyttäjien kiehtovaan elämään
content:
Pollinators represent an astonishingly diverse group of animals, many of which possess remarkable abilities despite their small size. Bees can count, bumblebees solve problems, and on distant islands, even lizards can pollinate flowers.

The  exhibition, which combines science and art, offers a wealth of information, stunning visuals, and fun activities for visitors of all ages. Guests can play interactive games like "Identify the Pollinators" and "Pollinator Protection Bingo," design their own imaginary pollinator, and explore the museum's impressive collection of specimens. The exhibition is based on a newly illustrated non-fiction book.

– We want to show the world through the eyes of pollinators, says exhibition scriptwriter Mia Rönkä, Adjunct Professor in Environmental Ecology at the University of Turku. Rönkä has written the exhibition’s informational texts and poems.

Although the sensory perceptions, cognitive abilities, and communication methods of pollinators like bees differ from ours as humans, we can still strive to understand and appreciate them as individuals of other species – without anthropomorphizing them, Rönkä explains.

title: Arkadiankadun siltaremontti aiheuttaa muutoksia liikennejärjestelyihin Luonnontieteellisen museon lähistöllä
content:
The renovation will start with the construction of temporary traffic arrangements from Wednesday 7 January onwards. The renovation is expected to be completed in late 2026.

A temporary bridge for pedestrians will be built on the east side of Arkadiankatu over the Baana. The aim is to maintain the pedestrian route on the east side of the bridge until the temporary bridge is operational. Cyclists will also be able to use the bridge.

The Baana route underneath the bridge is expected to remain open for most of the renovation's duration, with some minor exceptions.

There will be changes to the motor vehicle routes by the bridge and around it in January. If possible, should be favoured during the bridge renovation.

Connections to the bus terminals in Kamppi will remain available, but there will be a slight diversion of routes.

Trams 1 and 1T will run via Simonkatu and Kamppi. Lasipalatsi and the Natural History Museum will not be served.

The diversion is due to the renovation of the Arkadiankatu bridge and will remain in place until late 2026. The renovation will not affect HSL's bus services.

title: Ukrainan sota - yliopiston suositukset
content:
The University of Helsinki has condemned the military action by Russia and expressed its support for Ukraine and its university community. We have also expressed our support for Ukraine, together with other Finnish universities, through statements by and the . As a demonstration of support, we have illuminated buildings in the colours of the Ukrainian flag and raised the flag on our premises.

One of the principles of the University of Helsinki is to promote international collaboration in research and higher education, and to support these efforts even in difficult circumstances. Russia’s indefensible military aggression in Ukraine has required exceptional measures, which include those taken in the collaboration between universities.

The University of Helsinki is monitoring both national and EU-level sanctions, adapting our policies and processes accordingly. Together with other Finnish and international universities, the University of Helsinki strives to promote the end of military action in Ukraine, while supporting Ukrainian institutions and people.
